process: Choosing the prompt: Claude read the assignment and checked our real constraints: deadline, which data hosts were reachable, and existing tools. It then ran a six-agent panel. Three agents scoped one prompt each, and three judges scored the scopes as the grader, as a delivery lead and as a skeptical finance professor. The panel rated prompt 2 the safest. We chose prompt 1 because it was the most fun, and folded in the judges' warnings: test the math independently, never fake data, host on no-login pages, and fix the option-pricing bias.

Building: Claude (Anthropic's Claude Code) wrote the game engine, the user interface, the data downloader and the GitHub Actions automation from a plan we reviewed and approved. We made the product decisions (game design, ticker pool, branding) and did the GitHub settings, play-testing and review.

Testing: Claude wrote unit tests with hand-computed answers, an independent pandas recomputation of every metric on real data, and a browser test that plays the game through the UI. Running these caught real bugs during the build. One: the 5 bp trading cost made a maximum 150% long position fail the buying-power check. Another: chart axes lost their labels.

Adversarial review: after the first build, four separate AI agents audited it. One checked the finance math and looked for look-ahead bias, one tried to exploit or crash the game, and one played it as a first-time student on desktop, phone and dark mode. A fourth looked for what the first three missed. Every finding had to include a reproduction script or an exact code citation. Together they reported 35 findings, some overlapping. We reproduced each critical and major one, fixed it, wrote a regression test for it, and then reran the reviewers' own scripts against the fixed engine.
fixes: Options got around the leverage limits. Four 200% call legs gave about 8× delta exposure. Because Sharpe averages simple daily returns, a wiped-out account could even top the Sharpe ranking. Fix: net exposure (stock plus option delta) is capped at −100%/+150%, total option notional at 200% of equity, and a busted account has no Sharpe and ranks last.

Ranking by Sharpe alone misordered results. A +20%, 0.6%-drawdown account ranked below a −76% buy & hold. Fix: the overall rank is the average of the Sharpe, max-drawdown and IRR ranks, which matches the prompt's 'judged on all of' criteria.

Index calls were priced too rich. Every strike was priced at the VIX level, so a 5%-out-of-the-money SPY covered call beat SPY by 46 points. Fix: at-the-money index vol is 0.88 × VIX plus a volatility smile, steeper for the index. The SPY buy-write now roughly matches SPY, as real buy-write indexes did.

Written puts weren't truly cash-secured. Collateral was checked before the rest of the ticket, so the same cash could buy calls. Fix: the strike value must be covered by the cash left after the whole order.

Simply holding a 150% long was often blocked, and the autopilot crashed (in 79% of levered starts). The borrowing cap was being re-applied every month. Fix: limits apply to orders that add risk, and drift is policed by the 25% maintenance margin, now also checked on option-expiry days. Re-running the reviewer's script gave 0 crashes in 1,298 runs.
Autopilot rules didn't do what their labels said when they took over mid-game: 'T-bills only' kept your stock. Fixed and tested.

Data pipeline: a run during market hours could publish an intraday price as the close, and provider rounding noise caused no-op data commits that shifted replays by a few dollars. Fixed: unfinished bars are dropped, and published values are kept unless the provider truly re-adjusts them.

Usability and accessibility: opening the autopilot on a phone broke the layout, the phone scorecard was unreadable, replay links weren't validated, a double-click could skip a month, turn results weren't announced to screen readers, and the dark-mode button contrast was too low. All fixed.
Disclosed, not fixed: blind mode is honour-based, because a static site has to download the price file and anyone can see it in developer tools. Option prices are model prices, not historical quotes.
